questoes.pergunta: Which statement about the CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy is correct?
opcoes: Instructions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` apply only to that user, across their projects, and are not shared with teammates through version control.
Project-level instructions must live in `.claude/CLAUDE.md`; a `CLAUDE.md` file placed at the repository root is not read by Claude Code.
A `CLAUDE.md` in a subdirectory replaces the project-level file for any work that Claude does on files inside that particular subdirectory.
User-level instructions are copied into the project `CLAUDE.md` the first time a developer opens the repository with Claude Code.
questoes.explicacao: The hierarchy has three levels: user (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, personal), project (root `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, shared via version control) and directory (a `CLAUDE.md` in a subdirectory). User-level instructions never reach teammates through the repository, which is the root of many 'works on my machine' problems.
feedbacks: Correct. User-level instructions are personal and are not shared through version control.
Tempting because `.claude/` holds most configuration, but the project level accepts either `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or a root `CLAUDE.md`.
Tempting because the subdirectory file is more specific, but levels are combined, not replaced; the project instructions still apply.
Tempting because it would explain how personal rules spread, but nothing is copied; user-level files stay on that user's machine.

questoes.pergunta: Three senior developers get Claude Code to return `Result<T>` from domain services instead of throwing exceptions. A developer who joined this week cloned the same repository, and in his sessions Claude throws exceptions. The seniors' rule lives in each of their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Ask the new developer to copy one senior's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` to his machine, so that his sessions load the same instructions.
Move the rule into the project-level `CLAUDE.md` and commit it, so every developer who clones or pulls the repository receives it.
Restate the rule in capital letters at the top of each senior's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so that Claude treats it as a higher priority.
Create a `/result-pattern` skill in `.claude/skills/`, so the new developer can invoke the rule whenever he works on domain services.
questoes.explicacao: The rule is a team convention stored at the user level, which applies only to each senior and is not shared through version control. Moving it to the project-level CLAUDE.md fixes the hierarchy problem for the new hire and for every future teammate and CI run.
feedbacks: Tempting because it works immediately for one person, but it is manual, drifts over time and leaves the rule outside the repository.
Correct. A team convention belongs at the project level, versioned with the repository.
Tempting because emphasis sometimes helps adherence, but the new developer never loads that file at all, so emphasis changes nothing for him.
Tempting because skills are shared, but a skill loads only when invoked; a rule that should always apply belongs in CLAUDE.md.

questoes.pergunta: A developer reports that Claude Code followed the project's structured-logging conventions yesterday but ignores them in today's session, which she started from a different folder. A teammate's sessions behave correctly. What should she do first to diagnose this?
opcoes: Ask Claude in the session whether it has read the project `CLAUDE.md`, and trust its answer about which conventions are in effect.
Rewrite the logging conventions with more emphasis and examples, then restart the session to see whether the behavior improves.
Run the `/memory` command to check which memory files are loaded in this session, and compare them with her teammate's session.
Switch the session to a larger model, since inconsistent rule-following between sessions usually comes from limited model capacity.
questoes.explicacao: Inconsistent behavior across sessions is first a question of which instruction files are actually loaded. The `/memory` command shows the memory files in play for the session, so she can see whether the project file, a personal file or a directory-level file differs from her teammate's setup before changing any text.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is quick, but self-reported answers are not verification; the session's loaded files are what matter.
Tempting because clearer rules help, but if the file is not loaded, no rewrite will change the behavior; verify first.
Correct. `/memory` verifies which memory files are loaded and is the first diagnostic step for inconsistent behavior.
Tempting (the 'bigger model' distractor): the symptom follows the session's setup, not the model, so this skips the real check.

questoes.pergunta: A package's `CLAUDE.md` contains the line `@../../standards/payments-api.md`. What does this line do?
opcoes: It adds a link that Claude may decide to open later in the session if the payments standard seems relevant to the task at hand.
It registers `payments-api.md` as a slash command that developers working in that package can invoke as `/payments-api`.
It loads `payments-api.md` only when Claude edits files whose paths fall under the `standards/` directory of the repository.
It imports the content of `payments-api.md` into context with that `CLAUDE.md`, so the standard lives in one file and is reused.
questoes.explicacao: The `@` import syntax references an external file and brings its content into context together with the CLAUDE.md that contains the line. This keeps CLAUDE.md modular: a standard is written once and imported by each package that needs it.
feedbacks: Tempting because it looks like a hyperlink, but an import is expanded into context; it does not depend on Claude choosing to open it.
Tempting because slash commands are also Markdown files, but commands live in `.claude/commands/`; an `@` line is an import.
Tempting because it resembles path-scoped loading, but that is what `paths` frontmatter in `.claude/rules/` does, not imports.
Correct. `@` imports pull the referenced file into context alongside the importing CLAUDE.md.

questoes.pergunta: A developer wants a personal `/standup-notes` command that summarizes her commits for the daily stand-up. It should be available in every repository she works on and should not appear for her teammates. Where should she create it?
opcoes: In `~/.claude/commands/standup-notes.md` in her home folder, since user-scoped commands are personal and not versioned.
In `.claude/commands/standup-notes.md` in each repository, since commands placed there stay private to whoever wrote them.
In the project `CLAUDE.md` of each repository, under a 'Personal commands' heading that describes the summary she wants.
In `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, as a line that defines `/standup-notes`, since user-level memory files define personal commands.
questoes.explicacao: User-scoped commands live in `~/.claude/commands/` and are personal: available to that developer in all her projects and never shared through a repository. Project-scoped commands in `.claude/commands/` are the opposite, shared with everyone who clones the repository.
feedbacks: Correct. `~/.claude/commands/` holds personal commands that do not reach teammates.
Tempting because the file name is hers, but `.claude/commands/` is versioned with the repository, so every teammate would get the command.
Tempting because CLAUDE.md is where instructions go, but it does not define commands, and the project file is shared with the team.
Tempting because it is personal, but CLAUDE.md files hold instructions, not command definitions; commands are files in a commands directory.

questoes.pergunta: Your team wants a project skill named `release-check` that uses frontmatter options such as `context: fork` and `argument-hint`, shared through the repository. Which file defines it?
opcoes: `.claude/commands/release-check.json`, with `context`, `allowedTools` and `argumentHint` defined as JSON keys inside the file
`.claude/skills/release-check/SKILL.md`, with the options declared in the YAML frontmatter at the top of the Markdown file
`~/.claude/skills/release-check/SKILL.md`, because skill frontmatter is honored only for skills stored in each user's home
`.claude/rules/release-check.md`, with a `paths` field listing the files on which the release check should be triggered
questoes.explicacao: Project skills live in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, and the SKILL.md file supports YAML frontmatter options including `context: fork`, `allowed-tools` and `argument-hint`. Because it is in the repository, the skill is shared with the team.
feedbacks: Tempting because it lists the right options, but skills are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, not JSON files in the commands directory.
Correct. A project skill is `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter.
Tempting because personal skills also use SKILL.md, but this location is personal and not shared; frontmatter works in project skills too.
Tempting because rules also use frontmatter, but rules carry conventions that load by path; they are not invocable skills.

questoes.pergunta: Which statement about the `context: fork` option in a skill's frontmatter is correct?
opcoes: It creates a git worktree for the skill, so that any files the skill edits are kept apart from the developer's working copy.
It duplicates the current conversation into a second session, so the developer can compare two answers from the same skill.
It runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so verbose or exploratory output does not pollute the main conversation.
It reloads the skill file from disk on every turn, so that edits made to `SKILL.md` during a session take effect immediately.
questoes.explicacao: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context. Verbose output (such as a codebase analysis) or exploratory context (such as brainstorming alternatives) stays in that context, and only the result returns to the main session.
feedbacks: Tempting because 'fork' suggests version control, but the option isolates conversation context, not files.
Tempting because 'fork' suggests copying the session, but the sub-agent does not receive the conversation; it runs the skill on its own.
Correct. A forked skill runs in an isolated sub-agent and keeps its output out of the main conversation.
Tempting because it sounds like a refresh option, but `context: fork` is about where the skill runs, not how often it is read.

questoes.pergunta: A project skill generates API client boilerplate. It only needs to create and write files, but in one run it executed a shell command that deleted a generated folder containing hand-written code. Which frontmatter setting addresses this?
opcoes: `argument-hint`, listing the folders the skill may write to, so that Claude asks before touching anything outside of them
`context: fork`, so that the skill's shell commands run in an isolated sub-agent and cannot affect the developer's files
A `description` stating that the skill is non-destructive, so Claude avoids shell commands while the skill is running
`allowed-tools`, limited to file write operations, so that the skill cannot run shell commands while it is executing
questoes.explicacao: `allowed-tools` in skill frontmatter restricts tool access during the skill's execution. Limiting it to file write operations keeps a boilerplate generator from running destructive shell commands, which a prompt or description can only discourage.
feedbacks: Tempting because it names the folders, but `argument-hint` prompts for parameters; it does not limit what the skill can do.
Tempting because 'isolated' sounds safe, but `context: fork` isolates conversation context, not the file system.
Tempting because descriptions shape behavior, but wording is guidance, not a restriction on tools.
Correct. `allowed-tools` restricts the skill to the tools it needs, preventing destructive actions.

questoes.pergunta: Developers often invoke the team's `/triage-incident` skill without the incident ID it needs, and Claude then guesses the most recent incident. What is the most direct fix?
opcoes: Add `argument-hint` to the skill's frontmatter, so developers are prompted for the incident ID when they invoke it without one.
Add a line to the project `CLAUDE.md` telling developers to always pass the incident ID when they invoke the triage skill.
Add `context: fork` to the skill, so that the sub-agent can look up the correct incident ID before the triage begins.
Add `allowed-tools` to the skill, so it can query the incident tracker and pick the incident that it judges most urgent.
questoes.explicacao: `argument-hint` in skill frontmatter declares the expected argument so developers are prompted for the required parameter when they invoke the skill without it. That fixes the missing-ID problem at the point of invocation instead of letting Claude guess.
feedbacks: Correct. `argument-hint` prompts for the required parameter when the skill is invoked without arguments.
Tempting because it documents the requirement, but CLAUDE.md instructions are read by Claude, not shown to developers when they type the command.
Tempting because a sub-agent could search, but isolation does not tell it which incident the developer meant.
Tempting because it automates the choice, but letting Claude pick the incident is still guessing, just with more tools.

questoes.pergunta: Your team's `/gen-migration` skill in `.claude/skills/` produces terse output. You prefer a verbose version that explains each schema change, but your teammates like the current one. What should you do?
opcoes: Edit `.claude/skills/gen-migration/SKILL.md` to add the explanations, since teammates can simply skip over the extra text.
Create a personal copy in `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name, such as `gen-migration-verbose`, and edit that copy.
Add a section to the project `CLAUDE.md` asking Claude to explain each schema change whenever the skill runs for you.
Keep a personal branch of the repository with a modified `SKILL.md`, and rebase it whenever the team skill changes.
questoes.explicacao: Personal skill variants belong in `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name, so they do not affect teammates and do not compete with the team's skill. You keep both: the shared `/gen-migration` and your own `/gen-migration-verbose`.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is one edit, but changing the versioned skill changes it for the whole team.
Correct. A personal variant in `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name avoids affecting teammates.
Tempting because it looks targeted, but the project CLAUDE.md is shared and always loaded, so the instruction reaches everyone.
Tempting because it isolates your change, but it creates ongoing merge work for something the personal skills directory handles directly.

questoes.pergunta: Storybook files (`*.stories.tsx`) sit next to their components in 25 folders, and new folders are added every sprint. The team wants the same story-writing conventions applied whenever Claude edits any of them. Which approach is the most maintainable?
opcoes: Place a `CLAUDE.md` with the story conventions in each of the 25 folders, and add one to each new folder during code review.
Add a 'Stories' section to the root `CLAUDE.md`, and rely on Claude to apply it when the file being edited is a story file.
Create `.claude/rules/stories.md` with `paths: ["**/*.stories.tsx"]`, so the rule loads for story files in any folder.
Create a `/story-conventions` skill that developers invoke before they ask Claude to write or update a story file.
questoes.explicacao: Glob-pattern rules apply conventions by file type regardless of directory, so one rule covers all current and future folders. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are bound to their directories and must be duplicated, which is why path-specific rules are preferred for conventions spread across the codebase.
feedbacks: Tempting because it works per folder, but it duplicates the conventions 25 times and depends on reviewers remembering new folders.
Tempting because it is simple, but it loads for all work and relies on inference rather than explicit matching.
Correct. A `paths` glob by file type covers story files wherever they live, including new folders.
Tempting because skills are reusable, but they load on demand; automatic application needs a path-scoped rule.

questoes.pergunta: Which statement about a file in `.claude/rules/` whose YAML frontmatter has `paths: ["infra/**/*.tf"]` is correct?
opcoes: It loads at the start of every session, like `CLAUDE.md`, and the `paths` field only tells Claude where the conventions apply.
It loads only when a developer types the rule's file name as a slash command while working on the infrastructure files.
It loads only when the session is launched from inside the `infra/` directory, and stays out of sessions started elsewhere.
It loads when Claude works with a file matching the glob, so it adds no context while Claude edits unrelated files.
questoes.explicacao: A `paths` field with glob patterns makes the rule conditional: it loads only when Claude works with matching files. That keeps Terraform conventions out of context during unrelated work, reducing irrelevant context and token usage.
feedbacks: Tempting because rules without `paths` do load at startup, but adding `paths` is precisely what makes loading conditional.
Tempting because commands are also Markdown files, but rules are not invoked; they load by matching file paths.
Tempting because it sounds like directory scoping, but matching is based on the files Claude works with, not the launch folder.
Correct. Path-scoped rules load when matching files are worked on and stay out of unrelated work.

questoes.pergunta: Which TWO tasks are better suited to direct execution than to plan mode? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Choosing between event-driven and polling integration with a supplier, each with new infrastructure
Moving authorization checks from 30 controllers into one shared middleware component
Fixing the `NullReferenceException` that the stack trace points to at line 88 of `OrderService.cs`
Adding a conditional that rejects a booking whose end date falls before its start date
Migrating 52 files from one HTTP client library to another, including custom retry handlers
questoes.explicacao: Direct execution fits simple, well-scoped changes such as a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace or adding one date validation. Large migrations, cross-cutting refactors and choices between integration approaches with different infrastructure needs are what plan mode is designed for.
feedbacks: Tempting because it might be a small diff at first, but it is an architectural choice with different infrastructure requirements: plan mode.
Tempting because the pattern repeats, but it touches 30 controllers and changes a cross-cutting design: plan mode.
Correct. A single-file fix with a clear stack trace is a well-understood change with clear scope.
Correct. Adding one date validation conditional is a simple, well-scoped change.
Tempting because it is mechanical, but a migration across 52 files with custom handlers is large-scale and multi-file: plan mode.

questoes.pergunta: You need to migrate a .NET solution from `Newtonsoft.Json` to `System.Text.Json` across about 70 files, several with custom converters. Which workflow fits best?
opcoes: Use plan mode to investigate usages and agree on a migration plan, then switch to direct execution to implement the approved plan.
Stay in plan mode for the whole migration, so Claude re-plans each file before editing it and every single change gets reviewed.
Use direct execution from the start and let Claude migrate the files in alphabetical order, fixing compile errors as they appear.
Use direct execution for files without converters first, and enter plan mode later only if the converter files cause trouble.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode is for investigation and design; once a plan is approved, direct execution is the efficient way to carry it out. Combining them avoids both risks: committing to an approach before exploring, and paying planning overhead on every file of an already-planned migration.
feedbacks: Correct. Plan mode to investigate and plan, then direct execution to implement the planned approach.
Tempting because it maximizes review, but re-planning each file adds overhead once the approach is already decided.
Tempting because compile errors guide the work, but discovering the converter strategy file by file is the rework planning prevents.
Tempting because it starts with the easy part, but the converter complexity is known up front; postponing planning invites rework.

questoes.pergunta: During a multi-phase task, the discovery phase requires searching about 200 files to map how invoices are generated. How does the Explore subagent help?
opcoes: It reads files into the main conversation faster than Read, so discovery can finish before the context window fills up.
It runs the verbose discovery in its own context and returns a summary, so the main session keeps room for later phases.
It compresses the main conversation after each file is read, so earlier messages are summarized while discovery continues.
It switches the session into plan mode, so files read during discovery leave the context once the plan has been approved.
questoes.explicacao: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output in its own context and returns a summary, preserving the main conversation's context. In multi-phase tasks this prevents the discovery phase from exhausting the context window before planning and implementation.
feedbacks: Tempting because speed sounds helpful, but the problem is where the output lands, not how fast files are read.
Correct. Explore keeps verbose discovery in a separate context and hands back only the summary.
Tempting because it resembles `/compact`, but Explore does not summarize the main conversation; it keeps discovery out of it.
Tempting because exploring and planning go together, but Explore is a subagent, not a mode switch, and it is what keeps reads out of the main context.
